Introduction

Mr. Binoy Debbarma well-known personality in the arena of Kokborok literature. We have seen from our childhood who started writings from 1981. At that point of time the Kokborok was just recognized as state language of Tripura.

After that the Kokborok education started from the year 1984 onward. The important part to introduce any language needs written literature for education curriculum but there were other most important subjects need to coincide properly such as Spelling Method, Counting Method, Grammar, compilation of Dictionaries etc.

Publishing one Poem & one Short story books namely SONNET KOKLOPROK and NAKHRAI in the years 1988 & 1989 it has felt him shortage of Kokborok vocabulary in creating literature. Therefore it has lead to step up in collection & compilation of dictionaries and terminology in question of proper introduction of Kokborok education along with official uses of the Kokborok.

Accordingly the Anglo-Kokborok Dictionary was printed at Don Bosco Press, Shillong, Meghalaya and published in the year 1996 by KOHM Publication, Krishnanagar, Agartala and Kokborok Community Welfare Society, Arundhutinagar, Agartala. The fund was received the London Tear Fund for printing the dictionary through The NORTH EAST INDIA COMMITTEE ON RELIEF & DEVELOPMENT [NEICORD], Shalom, Laitumkhrah, Shillong, Meghalaya.

Mr. Shiddeshwar Prasad, His Excellency the Governor of Tripura was the chief guest of the dictionary release program. 

Second edition of Anglo-Kokborok Dictionary was published in the year 2002. Re-printing of the dictionary by changing the nomenclature as English-Kokborok-Bengali Dictionary as well as putting Bengali terms was published in  the year 2010. 

This third edition of English-Kokborok-Bengali Dictionary is going to publish where there will be all new Kokborok terminology in this edition created by both Literary Organizations and TTAADC.  

The Khurumpui Publications is going to start with his 10(ten) books. These are follows:
1. Ani Langmano Ang Rwktharwi [My Autobiography] 
2. Seven Pioneering Works 
3. Kokborokni Rangchak-richak [The ornamental terms and folk literature of the Kokborok]
4. The Counting Method of Kokborok 
5. Kokborok-English Kokrwbam [A Kokborok-English Dictionary]
6. English-Kokborok-Bengali Dictionary
7. Nakhrai [A collection of Kokborok Short stories]
8.  Tipra Dopha - kwmama, rutukma, songsama [A compilation of Kokborok articles] 
9. The Tipra People [A common identity of the Indigenous people of Tripura]
10. Easy Kokborok Learning Course.

Hope that Khurumpui Publications will make a remarkable journey in publication of Kokborok books with active participation and august appreciation of you all in the days to come.


Boyar Debbarma
Khurumpui Publications


































A brief outline of the Kokborok speaking Tipra people

The Kokborok was declared as state language of Tripura in the year 1979 AD. But it was supposed to be recognized as Tipra language which was ignored. The Tipra is the proper term to denote not only the language but the name of people and land which is far more historical, scientific and meaningful. 

The background of the Tipra language becaming Kokborok was started by confusion occurred on the basis of a grammar book titled Kokboroma compiled by Sri Cha Dhoulot Ahammad M M Dahar & Sri Cha Mahammad Ummor in the year of 1307 Tipra Era i.e. 1897 AD. After three years later, Radha Mohan Debbarma Thakur compiled another grammar book titled Kokborokma in the year of 1310 Tipra Era i.e. 1900 AD. Both the two book writers mentioned the Kokboroma and Kokborokma are the book of Troipur or Tipra Grammar.

The Tipra language was recognized as the Kokborok. Scholars from different walks came to visit this land & language coincided in different terms according to their tongue such as Troipur, Tippara, Tipperah, Tipura and Tripura.
 
It was only a French traveler Jean Baptiste Tavernier visited this land in the year 1640 who kept the authentic term of TIPRA which is still pronounce by the people. It was recorded in the travelling note titled Tavernier's Travells, translated in English by J. Philips, Book III, Part-II, Chapter XVI, Of the Kingdom of Tipra. The extract, "There is nothing in Tipra which is fit for strangers. There is a Mine of Gold, but the Gold is very coarse. And there is a sort of very coarse Silk, which is all the Revenue the King has. He exacts no Subsidies from his Subjects; but only that they, who are not of the prime Nobility, should work six days in a year in his Mine, or in his Silk-works. He sends his Gold and his Silk into China, for which they bring him back Silver, which he coins into pieces to the value of ten Sous, he also makes thin pieces of Gold, like the Aspers of Turkey; of which he has two sorts, four of the one sort making a Crown, and twelve of the other".   

There is another book titled TRAVELS IN INDIA, Volume I & II of Jean Baptiste Travenier translated from the original French Edition in 1676 with a biographical sketch of the Author, Notes, Appendices, etc by V. Ball, LLD, FRS, FGS, Director of the Science and Art Museum, Dublin.

It was the Tavernier who wrote the Tipra term properly as pronounced by the native people. There are two popular contents on the origin of the Tipra term. One is Twipra in long form Twi and bupra, the confluence of rivers and another is the King Tripur.

Rajmala, the chronicle of Tipra Kings compiled by Kailash Chandra Singha which was first published in 1896 AD. At the very first page, Tipra term was written which is corrupted in the present form of Tripura term. And it was first time the Tripura term was coincided in the Bengali language form.

The Tipra term is widely used by Suniti Kumar Chatterji in his famous book KIRATA JANA KRITI, first published in 1951. All information in regard to Tipra term is available at pages 130-139.

K. D. Menon, IAS, State Editor of Tripura District Gazettes has elaborated on Tipra term in Chapter-I, General: Introduction, Origin of the name of the District, Page-1, published in 1975 as quoted, "......It is relevant to note that even today the hill people pronounce the word as Tipra and not Tripura". 

The Tipra term was written in different pronunciation. Here are the time line of changing the names of land, people & language as Troipur, Tippara, Tipperah, Tipura and finally Tripura by different scholars in different period of time.
SlThe term & yearParticulars01.Troipur in 1458Troipur was named in Sanskrit in 1458 AD by Shukreshwar & Baneshwar in Srirajratnakaram. 02.Tippara in 1583Tippara was named by Ralph Fitch, a English traveler during his visit to India 1583-1591.03.Tipperah in 1841Tipperah was written during 1841 to 1902 AD by Sir A. Phayre, H. C. Sutherland, T. H. Lewin, W. W. Hunter, Rev. S. Endle, G. Campbell, J. D. Anderson. 04.Tripura in 1896Tripura was coincided by Kailash Chandra Singha in Rajmala in the year 1896 AD. 05.Tipura in 1903Tipura was written in the year 1903 AD by G. A. Grierson in his famous book titled Linguistic Survey of India. 
The Troipur 
May I throw some light on the history of written form of Kokborok which was previously known as Tipra language. We had evidence of more than five hundred years of written literature in this language. The Tipra King Darma Manikya during his reign 1431-1462 AD, two priests Shukhreswar and Baneswar Chakraborty were invited and they composed Srirajratnakaram in Sanskrit in the year 1458 AD. The term Srirajratnakaram translated as Ocean of Kings, is the first published chronological history of Tipra Royal Dynasty. In the 23-25 Slokas of Prothoma Sorgo of Srirajratnakaram, it is written that the court-poets collected their materials from Tipra language narrated by royal priest Chontai Durlobendro through King Darma Manikya for composing the book. In this compilation Tipra language was mentioned as Troipur language which is presently known as Kokborok. The verses go: "Ebang Chontayi Bochonong Shrutto Praho Noradipo, Oshthu Guhyotomong Tabodbruhi Troipur Bhasaya - 1/23. Chottaru Boyomtroibo Ponchomu No Hi Bidyote, Totha Rohosyong Srinumostomukhambujo Nisritom - 1/24. Mulong Jodbhobota Geyong Dhimong Troipur Bhasaya, Shukro Banesworui Tochho Tonutang Debo Bhasaya - 1/25".

It has distinctly narrated that the King told the original history and verses of Srirajratnakaram proves that Shukreswar and Baneswar Chakraborty composed Srirajratnakaram collecting from the Tipra language before 1458 AD. It is also said that the Chronicle was written in Tipra script called Kolma. In the later period, Kokborok was abandoned in Tipra royal court by the King Bir Chandra Manikya during the period of 1862-1896 AD and Bengali was declared Rajbhasha i.e. the court language. It was  tragic chapter that begin for the Kokborok in terms of losing their mother tongue in Tipra royal court.

The Tippara
English Traveler Ralph Fitch travelled India during 1583-1591 were composed English version of Early travels in India 1583-1619/ed. by William Foster(1863-1951) - London (u.a.) Milford, Oxford university press, 1921, it has clearly mentioned the word Tippara to Tipra term. I am quoting the website:www.payer.de/quellenkunde/quellen1504.htm. in page 11/14, ".........From Satagam I travelled by the country of the king of Tippara or Porto Grande, with whom the Mogores or Mogen have almost continuall warres". At foot note-6 it is written that Porto Grand was the Portuguese name for Chittagong. Tippara was a Kingdom now represented by the small state of Hill Tippera.   

The Tipperah 
Foreign scholars specifically British writers wrote the Tipra term as Tipperah or Tippera in their typical spelling during 1841 to 1902 AD by Sir A. Phayre, H. C. Sutherland, T. H. Lewin, E. T. Dalton, W. W. Hunter, Rev. S. Endle, G. Campbell and J. D. Anderson.

The Tipura 
One of the foreign scholars G. A. Grierson wrote the term Tipura in his book titled Linguistic Survey of India which was published in the year 1903. It was completely different with typical spelling of Tipperah written by other Englishmen.

The Tripura 
Present Bengalised term Tripura was first written by Kailash Chandra Singh in his book Rajmala in the year 1306 TE/1896 AD. This Tripura term was also written by Kali Prasanna Sen Vidyabhusan in his book Sri Rajmala in the year 1336 TE/1926 AD.

The Kokborok speaking Tipra people divided into numerous groups since inception which is linguistically better known as dialects. Presently Kokborok has 9(nine) groups or dialects having different Panji or Sandai i.e. Clan or Sub-dialect of the Kokborok speaking Tipra people. 
Nine Dialects or Groups are:
1. Debborma    	2. Jomatia    		3. Koloi    		
4. Murasing	 	5. Noatia 		6. Riang   
7. Rupini    		8. Tripura    		9. Uchoi.

Spelling method of Kokborok along with pronunciation of 6 vowels used in this Dictionary

1. KOKBOROK ALPHABETS
      A B C D E G H I J K L M N O P R S T U W Y
2. PRONUNCIATION OF VOWELS
      1. A, a as in Apple. In Kokborok, Apha - My Father
      2. E, e as in Emperor. In Kokborok, Er - To increase
      3. I, i as in Ink, In Kokborok, Isri - The Queen
      4. O, o as in Oblige. In Kokborok, Ok - The Belly
      5. U, u as in Utgard. In Kokborok, UI - Behind
      6. W, w as in (U) Wake. In Kokborok, Wng - To be
3. THE USES OF VOWEIS WITH THE CONSONANTS
      B+a is Ba, Example - Bara - Short
      B+e is Be, Example - Beng - The Spider
      B+i is Bi, Example -Bihik - His Wife
      B+o is Bo, Example - Bol - The Firewood
      B+u is Bu, Example - Bukung - The Nose
      B+w is Bw, Example - Bwlwng - Abundance
      All Consonant with Vowel will be used like this way.
4. REPRESENTION OF THE SOUND OF THE CONJOINT LETTERS
      Ch, Kh, N', Ng, Ph, Th, Ua, Uo
4.1       Ch + a is Cha - Right
      Ch + e is Cherep - Decrease
      Ch + i is Chirik - Shouting
      Ch + o is Chol - To cut
      Ch + u is Chuk - To high
      Ch + w is Chwk - To sting
      Kh, Ph, Th will be used in same way
4.2 	N' is the pronunciation of nasal sound
      Example: In' - The yes.
4.3 	Ng conjoint letter is generally used in the last syllable of a word
      Example: Aming - A Cat
                      Holong - The Stone
4.4 	Ua is used like this way
      Uak - Pig, Uah - Bamboo, Uatwi - Rain
4.5 	Uo is used like this way
      Thuo - Sleeping,  Buo - Beat
5. THE LAST ALPHABET OF A WORD BEARING K & P WILL BE G & B AFTER USING A VOWEL LETTER AS SUFFIX AND THE MEANING OF WORD WILL BE CHANGED.
Example:
1. 	Paithak - Last. Paithak + o - Paithago - In last
      Kok - Language. Kok+ o - Kogo - In language
2. 	Koklop - Poem. Koklop + o - Koklobo - In Poem
      Khaklap - Chest. Khaklap + o Khaklabo - In Chest
6. TO EXPLAIN THE HIGH TUNE OF A WORD, 'H' LETTER WILL BE FIXED WITH THE SYLLABLE WHEN THE HIGH TUNE IS PRONOUNCED
Example:
      Low Tune		High Tune
1. 	Lai - Easy		Laih - To cross
2. 	Bor - Scenceless	Bohr - To plant
3. 	Cha - To right		Chah - To eat
4. 	Nukhung - Family	Nukhuhng - The roof

Appendix - III

Tables of Money, Weight & Measures 
The English System 
Money
2 farthings	make	1 half penny
2 half pence or 4 farthings	"	1 penny
12 pence 	"	1 shilling
20 shillings	"	1 pound

Lineal Measure
3 barley corns	make	1 inch
12 inches	"	1 foot
3 feet	"	1 yard
51/2 yards                 	"	1 rod, pole or perch
40 poles or 220 yards	"	1 furlong
8 furlongs or 1760 yards	"	1 mile
3 miles	"	1 league

Standard Weight (Avoirdupois)
16 drams (dr.)	make	1 ounce (oz)
16 ounces	"	1 punds(lb)
28 pounds	"	1 quarter (qr)
4 quarter or 112 lbs.	" 	1 hundred weight (cwt) 	
20 hundred weights	"	1 ton
1 store = 14 Ibs.		1 cental = 100 lbs.

Square And Land Measure
144 sq. inches	make	1 sq.foot
9 sq. feet	"	1 sq. yard
30 1/4 sq. yards	"	1 sq. pole or rod.
16 sq. poles	"	1 sq. chain
40 sq. poles 	"	1 rood or 1210 sq. yds
4 roods or 10 sq. chains	" 	1 acre (4840 sq.yds)
1 cothah = 720 sq. ft. or 80 sq. yds.
1 bigha = 14400 sq. ft. or 1600 sq. yds.
1 acre = 3 1/40 bighas

The Metric System Money
10 centimes	make	1 decime
10 decimes	  "	1 franc

Lineal Measure
10 millimetres	make	1 centimetre
10 centimetres	"	1 decimetre
10 decimetres	"	1 metre
10 metres	"	1 decametre
10 decametres	"	1 hectometre
10 hectometres	"	1 kilogramme

Measures of Weight
10 milligrammes               	make	1 centigramme
10 centigrammes 	"	1 decigramme
10 decigrammes	"	1 gramme
10 grammes	"	1 decagramme
10 decagrammes	"	1 hectogramme
10 hectogrammes	"	1 kilogramme

The litre is the unit of the measures of capacity. It is the volume of a cubic decimetre.



Appendix - IV

Chemical Names of common Substances 
Alcohol = Ethyl Alcohol (C2H5OH)
Alum = Potassium Aluminium Sulphate (K2SO4,AIl2[SO4]324H2O)
Aqua fortis = Nitric Acid (HNO3)
Bi-Carbonate of Soda = Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate (NaHCO3)
Blue Vitriol (Blue Stone) = Copper Sulphate (CuSO4, 5H2O)
Boracic Acid = Boric Acid (H3BO3)
Borax = Sodium Borate (Na2B4O7, 10H2O)
Calomel = Mercurous Chloride (Hg2Cl2) (Laxative, non poisonous)
Chalk = Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3) [NaCl)
Common Salt = Sodium Chloride Corrosive Sublimate = Mercuric Chloride (HgCl2) (violently poisonous). (MgSO4, 7H2, O)
Epsom Salts = Magnesium Sulphate Fire Damp = Methane (CH4) + air.
Glauber Salts = Sodium Sulphate (Na2SO4,10H2O)
Green Vitriol = Ferrous Sulphate (FeSO4, 7 H2O)
Hypo = Sodium Thiosulphate (Na2S2O3, 5H2O)
Lime = Calcium Oxide (CaO)
Oil of Vitriol = Sulphuric Acid (H2SO4)
Plaster of Paris = Calcium Sulphate (CaSO4)2H2O).
Red Lead = Triplumbic Tetroxide (Pb3O4)
Sal Ammoniac = Ammonium Chloride (NH4Cl)
Sal volatile = Impure Ammonium Carbonate ([NH4]2CO2)
Saltpetre = Potassium Nitrate (KNO3)
Salts of Lemon = Potassium Hydrogen Oxalate (KHC2O4)
Spirit of Salt = Hydrochloric Acid (HCl)
Sugar of Lead = Lead Acetate (Pb[C2H3O2]2, 3H2O)
Verdigris= Basic Copper Acetate (-Cu[C2H3O2], Cu[OH]2)
Vinegar = Dilute Acetic Acid (C2H4O2)
Washing Soda = Crystalline Sodium Carbonate (Na2CO3, 10 H2O)
White Lead = Basic Lead Carbonate (2PbCO3, Pb[OH]2)

Appendix - XI  

The Calendar of Tipra Era [Tipra Bisikhong]
The calendar of Tipra Era (It is alson known as Tripura Era or Tring) based on the collected data from the different sources and distinguished persons who are attended in a seminar on Tipra Era which was organized by the Tripura Tribal Socio-Cultural Development Organization(TTSCDO) and Chethuang Literary Group on December 01, 1991 at Tripura Public Service Commission Hall, Agartala. A book namely The Historical Background of Tipra Era has been published by KOKBOROK TEI HUKUMU MISSION. 

It is to note that the 118th Tipra King Himti alias Jujarupha alias Hamtorpha introduced the Tipra Era to commorate the victory of a part of Bongodesh in the year 590 AD ie.512 SE.

In the Tipra Era Calendar, Talhing is the first month i.e.1st Talhing is starts on the 22nd December of Gregorian Calendar in every year and the normal year would consist of 365 days with 366 days for every leap year.
          
The following is the length of different months of Tipra Era Calendar with beginning date of month of the Gregorian Calendar:

Appendix - XII 

Kokborok Counting Method - newly adopted]  
The modified counting method of Kokborok has been finalized by the participants of the Kokborok Terminology Workshop after a threadbare discussion held during 14-18 May 2018 which was organized by Language Wing, Education Department, TTAADC at Kokborok Library Hall, Khumulwng, Tripura. A draft of the modified Kokborok Counting Method has been prepared by Mr. Binoy Debbarma, Senior Linguistic Officer of Language Wing, Education Department, TTAADC.

Background
In the decades of eighties the Kokborok counting method was adopted in the form of decimal system. It has coincided by putting the Chi figure i.e. Ten before Nwi, Tham, Brwi, Ba, Dok, Sni, Char and Chuku to count the Twenty, Thirty, Forty, Fifty, Sixty, Seventy, Eighty & Ninety. As a result, it has counting in the way of Two ten is Nwichi, Three ten-Thamchi, Four ten-Brwichi, Five ten-Bachi, Six ten-Dokchi, Seven ten-Snichi, Eight ten-Charchi and Nine ten-Chukuchi.

Therefore, it has pronouncing the counting of two figure of Nwi & chi - Nwichi, Tham & chi - Thamchi, Brwi & chi - Brwichi, Ba & chi - Bachi, Dok & chi - Dokchi, Sni & chi - Snichi, Char & chi - Charchi, Chuku & chi - Chukuchi but it is not the compact form for which has made single term of English like the Twenty, Thirty, Forty, Fifty, Sixty, Seventy, Eighty & Ninety. These are look like the follows: 
The Kokborok				The English
Chi 						Ten
Nwi chi (Two ten) is the Nwichi 		Two ten is the Twenty		
Tham chi (Three ten) is the Thamchi		Three ten is the Thirty		
Brwi chi (Four ten) is the Brwichi 		Four ten is the Forty		
Ba chi (Five ten) is the Bachi			Five ten is the Fifty		
Dok chi (Six ten) is the Dokchi 		Six ten is the Sixty		
Sni chi (Seven ten) is the Snichi		Seven ten is the Seventy	
Char chi (Eight ten) is the Charchi		Eight ten is the Eighty		
Chuku chi (Nine ten) is the Chukuchi		Nine ten is the Ninety		

Looking into the incomplete shape of compact figures, we may take the Pe from the traditional counting method of Kokborok where it has putting Pe with the Khol i.e. Twenty unit for counting the 21(Twentyone) to 30(Thirty) figures. These are the 21-Kholpesa, 22-Kholpenwi, 23-Kholpetham, 24-Kholpebrwi, 25-Kholpeba, 26-Kholpedok, 27-Kholpesni, 28-Kholpechar, 29-Kholpechuku and 30-Kholpechi. 

The counting of 31(thirty one) as Kholpechisa have a problem as the Kholpechisa denotes the 30(Thirty) itself because it is one time of Kholpechi. Accordingly the 32(thirty two) would not be Kholpechinwi because if we do not put Pe for nutrilizing in between Kholpechi & Nwi it will multiply and counting figure would be two time of Kholpechi or thirty i.e. 60(Sixty) but not 32(Thirty two).

On the other hand Forty is the Kholnwi i.e. two time of twenty according to the Khol based counting system. The Kholnwisa would not be Forty one but it is one time of Kholnwi i.e. Forty itself. The same thing would be happened if we do not put Pe for nutrilizing in between Kholnwi and Nwi i.e. the Kholnwinwi will be 80(Eighty) but not 42(Forty two).

The 50(Fifty) is counted as Kholnwichi i.e. two time of twenty plus Ten and the actual meaning of Kholnwichi would be ten time of Forty i.e. 400(Four hundred).  

Therefore, the twenty unit counting in Kokborok must be avoided for maintaining the scientific counting of the Kokborok. Particularly Khol term must be remained in Kokborok as synonym of Twenty only.

Suggestion for putting the Pe with the Two, Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight & Nine for counting the Twenty, Thirty, Forty, Fifty, Sixty, Seventy, Eighty & Ninety in Kokborok having Chi silence between counting unit figures & Pe has been acdopted The counting terminology will stand like these: 
English		Previous terms	Adopted Kokborok terms
20 - Twenty		Nwichi			Nwipe 		
30 - Thirty		Thamchi 		Thampe		
40 - Forty		Brwichi		Brwipe		
50 - Fifty		Bachi			Bape			
60 - Sixty		Dokchi			Dokpe		
70 - Seventy		Snichi			Snipe		
80 - Eighty		Charchi		Charpe		
90 - Ninety		Chukuchi		Chukupe

The terms presently used in Kokborok are One - Sa, Ten - Chi, Hundred - Ra, Thousand - Sai, Ojut - Chisai, Lakh - Rasai and Crore - Rwjag. 
The NumberThe termsKokborok(Presently in use)1OneSa10TenChi100HundredRa1,000ThousandSai10,000Ojut (Ten thousand)Chisai100,000LakhRasai10,000,000CroreRwjag 
After a threadbare discussion among the participants of the Kokborok Terminology Workshop   following terms of the Ojut, Lakh, Million, Billion and Trillion has been coincided and adopted are given below:
The numberThe termAccepted Kokborok term10,000Ojut(Ten thousand)Thwlwng100,000LakhRwbam 1,000,000Million - ten lakh in India.Burung 100,000,000Billion - hundred crore or a thousand millions  of French & U.S.A.Hayung 1,000,000,000,000 Trillion of U.S.A. & French - a thousand billion or a million millions.Nokhayung 1,000,000,000,000,000,000Trillion of U.K. & Germany - million million millions.
The Ojut & Lakh in Kokborok was previously coincided as Chisai & Rasai i.e. Ten thousand & Hundred thousand has been adopted with single term as Thwlwng and Rwbam. The detailed of the Counting Method of Ojut, Lakh, Million, Crore, Billion and Trillion in Kokborok are follows:

Appendix - XIII

Tipra Kinship [Tipra Halok]
01. Ang - I

02. Bachwi - Older sister-in-law ; wife of older brother
	Angbachwi - My older sister-in-law
	Nwbachwi - Your older sister-in-law
	Bubachwi - His ; Her older sister-in-law

03. Bai - Older sister
	Abi ; Aibi - My older sister
	Nibi - Your older sister
	Bibi - His ; Her older sister.

04. Baithang - Self

05. Bakoto(Bato) - Father of grandfather/grandmother

06. Bayung - Nephew
	Angbayung - My nephew
	Nwbayung - Your nephew
	Bubayung - His ; Her nephew

07. Bayungjwk - Niece
	Angbayungjwk - My niece
	Nwbayungjwk - Your niece
	Bubayungjwk - His ; Her niece

09. Bohrok - They

10. Bohrokno - Them

11. Bora - Grandson of son

12. Bukhuk - Sister in general

13. Chamai - Father-in-law of son or daughter
	Angchamai - Father-in-law of my son or daughter
	Nwchamai - Father-in-law of your son or daughter
	Bwchamai - Father-in-law of his / her son or daughter

14. Chamaijwk - Mother-in-law of son or daughter
	Angchamaijwk - Mother-in-law of my son or daughter
	Nwchamaijwk - Mother-in-law of your son or daughter
	Bwchamaijwk - Mother-in-law of hsi / her son or daughter

	Achu - My grandfather
	Nuchu - Your grandfather
	Buchu - His ; her grandfather

17. Chuk - Grandfather of grandfather

18. Chukhru-seklai - the sons or daughter of the same grand father.

19. Chukra - Previous generation to grandfather of grandfather or fifth 		Ascendent.

	Nwchwi - Your grandmother
	Bwchwi - His ; her grandmother

26. Dongoi - Addressed by wife to her hunband

27. Dongoiti - Addressed by husband to his wife

28. Halok - Relationship

29. Hamjwk - Bride

	Nahanok - Your younger sister
	Bahanok - His ; her younger sister

	Bihik - His wife

	Nukumui - Husband of his ; her older sister

Appendix - XIV 

The name of Gods & Devils [Mwtai-Atai]
1. Kharchi [The Fourteen God & Godess]
      Kokborok Name		Converted Name
01) Ama (Hakwchar Ama)	Hara (Shankar) 
02) Sangrongma		Uma (Shankari)
03) Mailuma			Hari (Bishnu)
04) Khumuma		Ma (Laxmi)
05) Twima			Bani (Bagdebi)
06) Hachwkma (Haichukma)	Kumar (Kartikeya)
07) Noksuma			Ganapa (Ganesh)
08) Ker			Bidhi (Brahma)
09) Nakri			Kha (Prithivi)
10) Lampra 			Abdhi (Samudra) 			
11) Akhata			Ganga (Bhagirathi)
12) Bikhata			Sikhi (Agni) 
13) Kalaiya			Kam (Pradhyum)
14) Goria			Himadri (Himayala Parbat)

2. The Priests of Kharchi 
01) Chontai (Okra) - Head Priest 
02) Naran (Yakchu) - Second Priest
03) Khapangtwi (Tukurinai) - Priest who wash & clean 
04) Galim (Tannai) -  Priest of Immolator
05) Bariphang (Pharnai- sipnai) - Priest who clean the premises

** Now a days, the Kharchi Nokthar (Temple) is situated at Aguli Kwcham (old Agartala) i.e. Khayerpur. It is worshiped on the eighth day of bright fortnight of the month of Talrung of Tipra Bisi and continued for seven days. After conversion into the Hindu deity it has counted according to the lunar year counting system.

3. The Priest of Goria 
01. Bogla Biyagnang - Priest who remains all time with Goria having legs.  
02. Bogla Biyakwrwi - Priest who remains all time with Goria having no legs.
03. Doria Biyagnang - Priest who play drum of Goria having legs
04. Doria Biyakwrwi - Priest who paly drum of Goria having no legs.
05. Kherphang Biyagnang - Head Priest of Goria having legs.
06. Kherphang Biyakwrwi - Head Priest of Goria having no legs.
07. Mwtaibalnai Biyagnang - Priest who carrying the Goria having legs. 
08. Mwtaibalnai Biyakwrwi - Priest who carrying the Goria having no legs.
      
** The Goria - a victory festival become a deity of the Tipra people which is worshiped on the first day of Taltung of Tipra Bisi which is falls on 21 April of Gregorian calendar but the workship is started seven days before on 24 Tallang of Tipra Bisi which called the Buisu festival i.e. on 14 April of Gregorian calendar.
      
The Devils in Kokborok
01. Burasa - name of a traditional deity of Tipra people
02. Deur - name  of a traditional deity of Tripra people
03. Hakosok - name of a traditional deity of Tipra people
04. Kebengrok (Thumnairok-Bonirok) -name of two traditional deity of Tipra people
05. Nusukari - name of a traditional deity of Tipra people 
06. Phara - Ghost 
07. Srijodu - name of a traditional deity of Tipra people
08. Srijomdu - name of a traditional deity of Tipra people
09. Swkal ; Swkaljwk - Witch 
      
1. The Priest of the traditional Deities
01. Ochai (Okra) - Head Priest
02. Barua ; Tolua (Yakchu) - Second/Helper Priest
03. Diyari Karnai - Priest who examine the presence of Devils in human body.
04. Khuritokhai - Priest who examine the presence of Devils in human body by a     particular way of stick playing.

Appendix - XVIII 

Different types wearing of Garment [Kanmung-Chummung]
01. Bangbaijaknai ; Twihjaknai - Wearing on the upper portion of body specially of  women.
      1) Rikutu - Cloth used on upper portion of body by women.
02. Berjaknai ; Borjaknai ; Yohrjaknai - Wearing in bum.
      1) Khum (khajuo) - Flower.
      2) Surang - Ornament used in bum.
03. Chumjaknai - Wearing of upper portion of body.
      1) Chador - Light Shawl. 
      2) Dulai - Shawl.
      3) Kamchwlwi - Shirt. 
      4) Kamchwlwiborok - Borok shirt.
      5) Kutai - Shirt. 
      6) Niyali ; Rijai - Quilt. 
      7) Rijai ; Niyali - Quilt.
      8) Ritrak - Borok Shawl. 
04. Hungjaknai - Wearing on the head without touch head.
      1) Hungkhung ; Sakau - Umbrella.
      2) Lakhuk - Traditional umbrella made of bamboo cane long size.
      3) Patla - Traditional umbrella made by bamboo cane rouind size.
      4) Sakau ; Hungkhung - Umbrella.
05. Kahjaknai - Wearing of shoes etc.
      1) Kahdong - Stilt. 
      2) Yaklap - Shoes. 
06. Kanjaknai - Wearing of lower portion of body.
      1) Changduk - Threads bind in middle.
      2) Kamsa ; Gamsa - Cloth for wearing lower portion of body for men.
      3) Kamsoi - Cloth for wearing lower portion of body for men.
      4) Kanrwbai - Ornament.
      5) Ribwsa - Small cloth. 
      6) Rignai - Garment weared in lower portion of women. 
      7) Rituku - Cloth used for taking bath.
07. Khachijaknai - Wearing by hanging.
      1) Kholja - Bag 
08. Phahnjaknai - Wearing by one fold binding specially in the neck of man.
      1) Rimai - Cloth used for their traditional identification of men.
      2) Rimaikutung - Cloth used in neck at winter.
09. Sorjaknai - Wearing by binding specially on head and breast of woman.
      1) Pakuri - Turbun
      2) Risa - Cloth of breast cover
10. Thupjaknai - Wearing by covering a part of body like googols, gloves and socks etc.  
      1) Mokholop - Gogols 
      2) Yakholop ; Yakmoja - Golves
      3) Yakmoja ; Yakholop - Socks
